name: Degree-Adjective-Indefinite (Big Mess Construction)

1.definition: Degree word and adjective precede the indefinite article, expressing degree or extent of the adjectival property
1.details: A degree-marked adjective phrase, including certain comparatives, precedes the indefinite article, inverting the normal order (cf. "a big mess" → "how big a mess"). Only compatible with indefinite "a(n)", not definite "the" (*"how big the mess"). The "how" variant can function as an interrogative phrase, fronting to clause-initial position. Variants differ in register. An intervening of is especially familiar in North American varieties and is more available with some degree phrases than others.

examples.form: It was [too big a problem] to ignore.
She's [so good a student] that she skipped a year.
It's not [as big a deal] as you think.
I've never seen [so big a crowd].
examples.note: "So" variant; more literary than other degree words

examples.form: It's not [that big of a deal].
examples.note: Of-insertion variant; common in North American English

examples.form: [more interesting a job] than I thought
examples.note: Published comparison. The fronted adjective phrase is comparative.

constraints.description: Eligible phrases include those with how, so, too, that and as and certain comparatives. Ordinary very uses a different word order.
Article must be indefinite a(n); definite the is ungrammatical
"How" variant can be interrogative, fronting to clause-initial position
Acceptability and register depend on the degree phrase and the availability of the intervening of variant.

dimensions.form: Degree word + adjective + indefinite article + noun
dimensions.meaning: Expresses degree/extent of adjectival property; scalar semantics
dimensions.distribution: Common in speech and writing; competes with such a big N and a N that big

projection.target: An eligible degree phrase can precede a in too serious a problem. Ordinary very yields a very serious problem. Comparatives are also documented, and acceptability of of varies with the particular degree expression and variety.
projection.evidence: The FrameNet chapter gives the comparatives alongside so, as, how, that and too. It explicitly leaves the distribution of intervening of open.

curious.title: How big a mess, too big a problem
curious.summary: With words like how, too, so, that and as, the adjective can move in front of a or an.
curious.body: In a big mess, the adjective sits between a and the noun. But after words such as how, so, too, that and as, the adjective moves forward and a follows it. So we say how big a mess, too big a problem, so good a student, not that good a teacher. The word a or an has to stay: this pattern doesn't work with the. In some varieties you can also add of, as in that big of a deal, though whether of is acceptable depends on the degree word and the variety. The ordinary word very doesn't do this, and takes the usual order: a very serious problem.

examples.text: It was [too big a problem] to ignore.
She's [so good a student] that she skipped a year.
It's not [as big a deal] as you think.

curious.try: Start from a big mess and ask how big a mess. Then try the same with the, and see whether it still works.

teacher.summary: Explains inverted order after degree words (how big a mess) and the a(n)-only restriction.
teacher.explain: A degree word plus an adjective can precede the indefinite article, reversing the usual order: a big mess becomes how big a mess. Eligible phrases include those with how, so, too, that and as, and certain comparatives (more interesting a job). The article must be indefinite a(n); the doesn't fit, as in how big the mess. The how version can be an interrogative phrase, fronted to the start of the clause. Ordinary very uses a different word order (a very serious problem). An intervening of (that big of a deal) is especially familiar in North American varieties and is more available with some degree words than others. Register differs among the variants.
teacher.terms: Degree word: a word such as how, so, too or as that modifies the adjective. Indefinite article: a or an, the words CGEL classes as determinatives.

examples.text: It was [too big a problem] to ignore.
It's not [that big of a deal].
[more interesting a job] than I thought

contrasts.note: Ordinary order, with the adjective after a.
This dictionary stars this version with the.

watch_for: A learner might put the definite article into the pattern, as in how big the mess.
A learner might expect very to behave like how and so, and move the adjective in front of a.
A learner might assume that of is available with every degree word, though this dictionary notes this varies with the degree word and variety.
teacher.activity: Give students a big mess, a good teacher and a serious problem. They build how, too, so and as versions, then check each with a different noun and say which degree words they can use.
